On almost perfect additive complements

Wouter van Doorn, Boning Liu, Quanyu Tang
Abstract.

Let A,BA,B be infinite sets of non-negative integers with n∈A+Bn\in A+B for all sufficiently large integers nn. We prove that if A⁡(x)​B​(x)−xA(x)B(x)-x does not tend to infinity, then

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x∈[32,2].\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\in\Big[\frac{3}{2},2\Big].

The lower bound is sharp, and confirms a conjecture of Chen. Our proof is based on the weak limits and the convolution factorization theorem of Gabardo and Lai. A discrete proof of the same bound was also given by Zhang. Motivated by the known spectrum of perfect additive complements, we conjecture that the interval (3/2,8/5)(3/2,8/5) is also excluded for almost perfect additive complements.

Key words and phrases: 
Additive Complements, Sumset, Difference
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11B13, 11B34

1. Introduction

Let A,BA,B be two subsets of non-negative integers, and A⁡(x),B⁡(x)A(x),B(x) be the corresponding counting functions defined by

A⁡(x):=∑a∈A0⩽a⩽x1,B⁡(x):=∑b∈B0⩽b⩽x1.A(x):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in A\\ 0\leqslant a\leqslant x\end{subarray}}1,\ B(x):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}b\in B\\ 0\leqslant b\leqslant x\end{subarray}}1.
  • •

    A,BA,B are called infinite, if A,BA,B are both infinite sets.

  • •

    A,BA,B are called additive complements, if each sufficiently large integer nn can be written as n=a+bn=a+b for a∈A,b∈Ba\in A,b\in B.

  • •

    Additive complements A,BA,B are called almost perfect, if A⁡(x)​B​(x)−x↛∞A(x)B(x)-x\not\to\infty.

  • •

    Additive complements A,BA,B are called perfect, if the expression n=a+bn=a+b is unique for all n∈ℤ⩾0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}.

For infinite additive complements, Sárközy and Szemerédi [12] proved Danzer’s conjecture[6]:

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x⩽1⟹A⁡(x)​B​(x)−x→∞.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\leqslant 1\implies A(x)B(x)-x\to\infty.

The problems were studied by many authors [6, 7, 11, 12]. Chen and Fang [2, 3, 4, 5] extended the result to show that for infinite almost perfect additive complements A,BA,B,

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x∈[3−3,2].\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\in[3-\sqrt{3},2].

Yang and Zhao [14] improved the lower bound to 4/34/3 recently. Chen conjectured that the lower bound of the interval should be 3/23/2, which is a sharp bound. In this paper, we confirm Chen’s conjecture. The proof is shown in Section 3.

Theorem 1.1 (Chen’s conjecture).

If A,BA,B are infinite almost perfect additive complements, then

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x∈[32,2].\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\in\Big[\frac{3}{2},2\Big].

For perfect additive complements, Bárány, Fang and Sándor [1] obtained a detailed description of the spectrum, including the gap stated below. In Section 4 we give an elementary proof for this gap, which also motivates Conjecture 1.3.

Theorem 1.2.

If A,BA,B are infinite perfect additive complements, then

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x∈{32}∪[85,2].\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\in\Big\{\frac{3}{2}\Big\}\cup\Big[\frac{8}{5},2\Big].
Conjecture 1.3.

If A,BA,B are infinite almost perfect additive complements, then

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x∈{32}∪[85,2].\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\in\Big\{\frac{3}{2}\Big\}\cup\Big[\frac{8}{5},2\Big].

Use of AI tools

We independently proved Theorem 4.5, which led us to consider a more general conjecture. ChatGPT 5.6 Pro identified the applicability of the result of Gabardo and Lai [9] and generated an initial proof of Chen’s conjecture (Theorem 1.1). We checked the proof and gave a refined version. The initial AI-generated proof has also been formalized and verified in Lean. The original proof and its Lean formalization are available in [13].

For μ\mu a nonzero finite positive Borel measure with compact support, define the left and right endpoints of its support by

ℓμ=min⁡supp​μ,rμ=max⁡supp​μ.\ell_{\mu}=\min\mathrm{supp}\,\mu,\ r_{\mu}=\max\mathrm{supp}\ \mu.
Lemma 2.3.

Let μ,ν\mu,\nu be two nonzero finite positive Borel measures with compact supports. Then

ℓμ∗ν=ℓμ+ℓν,rμ∗ν=rμ+rν.\ell_{\mu*\nu}=\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu},\,r_{\mu*\nu}=r_{\mu}+r_{\nu}.
Proof.

By the definition we have

(2.5) ℓμ∗ν⩾ℓμ+ℓν.\ell_{\mu*\nu}\geqslant\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu}.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, ℓμ∈supp​μ\ell_{\mu}\in\mathrm{supp}\ \mu and ℓν∈supp​ν\ell_{\nu}\in\mathrm{supp}\ \nu imply

μ([ℓμ,ℓμ+ε))>0,ν([ℓν,ℓν+ε))>0,\mu([\ell_{\mu},\ell_{\mu}+\varepsilon))>0,\ \nu([\ell_{\nu},\ell_{\nu}+\varepsilon))>0,

from which we find

(μ∗ν)([ℓμ+ℓν,ℓμ+ℓν+2ε))⩾μ([ℓμ,ℓμ+ε))ν([ℓν,ℓν+ε))>0.(\mu*\nu)([\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu},\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu}+2\varepsilon))\geqslant\mu([\ell_{\mu},\ell_{\mu}+\varepsilon))\nu([\ell_{\nu},\ell_{\nu}+\varepsilon))>0.

That is, any small open neighbourhood of ℓμ+ℓν\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu} has a positive measure. Hence ℓμ+ℓν∈supp⁡(μ∗ν)\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu}\in\mathrm{supp}(\mu*\nu), and

(2.6) ℓμ∗ν⩽ℓμ+ℓν.\ell_{\mu*\nu}\leqslant\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu}.

Combining this with (2.5), we have ℓμ∗ν=ℓμ+ℓν\ell_{\mu*\nu}=\ell_{\mu}+\ell_{\nu}. The case for rμ∗νr_{\mu*\nu} follows similarly. ∎

Let ℒE\mathcal{L}_{E} be normalized Lebesgue measure supported on the given Borel set EE of finite positive Lebesgue measure. Particularly, ℒ[0,1]\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]} is the standard Lebesgue measure on [0,1][0,1]. Let δx\delta_{x} be the Dirac measure at the point xx.

Let μ,ν\mu,\nu be two Borel probability measures supported on [0,1][0,1]. (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) is called a complementary pair of measures with respect to ℒ[0,1]\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]} if

μ∗ν=ℒ[0,1].\mu*\nu=\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]}.

Particularly, we have the trivial complementary pair (μ,ν)=(δ0,ℒ[0,1])(\mu,\nu)=(\delta_{0},\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]}) and (ℒ[0,1],δ0)(\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]},\delta_{0}).

In 2014, Gabardo and Lai [9, Thm 2.2] completely decided the structure of complementary pair with respect to ℒ[0,1]\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]}. We use their first two factors of the decomposition for Lemma 2.5.

Theorem 2.4 (Gabardo–Lai, 2014).

Let (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) be a non-trivial complementary pair of measures with respect to ℒ[0,1]\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]}, then there exist integers M1,M2⩾2M_{1},M_{2}\geqslant 2 and Borel probability measures μ′,ν′\mu^{\prime},\nu^{\prime} supported in [0,(M1​M2)−1][0,(M_{1}M_{2})^{-1}] with μ′∗ν′=ℒ[0,1M1​M2]\mu^{\prime}*\nu^{\prime}=\mathcal{L}_{[0,\frac{1}{M_{1}M_{2}}]}, such that either

μ=(1M1​∑j=0M1−1δjM1)∗μ′,ν=(1M2​∑j=0M2−1δjM1​M2)∗ν′,\mu=\Big(\frac{1}{M_{1}}\sum_{j=0}^{M_{1}-1}\delta_{\frac{j}{M_{1}}}\Big)*\mu^{\prime},\ \nu=\Big(\frac{1}{M_{2}}\sum_{j=0}^{M_{2}-1}\delta_{\frac{j}{M_{1}M_{2}}}\Big)*\nu^{\prime},

or μ,ν\mu,\nu interchanged.

Lemma 2.5.

Let (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) be a non-trivial complementary pair of measures with respect to ℒ[0,1]\mathcal{L}_{[0,1]}, then there exists t1,t2∈(0,1)t_{1},t_{2}\in(0,1) such that

max⁡{μ⁡([0,t1])​ν​([0,t1])t1,μ⁡([0,t2])​ν​([0,t2])t2}⩾32.\max\Big\{\frac{\mu([0,t_{1}])\nu([0,t_{1}])}{t_{1}},\frac{\mu([0,t_{2}])\nu([0,t_{2}])}{t_{2}}\Big\}\geqslant\frac{3}{2}.

4. Perfect additive complements

Recall that A,BA,B are called perfect additive complements, if A,BA,B are additive complements with r⁡(n)=1r(n)=1 for all n∈ℤ⩾0n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 0}. We will give an example of perfect additive complements. The mixed-radix construction was investigated by Ma [10] and developed by Fang and Sándor [8]. We independently discovered and studied the example.

={ε1+ε3​d1​d2+ε5​d1​d2​d3​d4+…}.\displaystyle=\Big\{\varepsilon_{1}+\varepsilon_{3}d_{1}d_{2}+\varepsilon_{5}d_{1}d_{2}d_{3}d_{4}+\ldots\Big\}.

5. Remarks

5.1. The terminology

It is true, but not trivial that all perfect additive complements are almost perfect additive complements. The claim can be derived from the argument in Section 4.

There exist non-trivial infinite almost perfect additive complements which are not perfect. Let mm be an integer, and C,D⊆{0,1,…,m−1}C,D\subseteq\{0,1,\ldots,m-1\} with 0∈C∩D0\in C\cap D and the map

C×D\displaystyle C\times D →ℤ/m​ℤ\displaystyle\to\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}
(c,d)\displaystyle(c,d) ↦c+d​mod​m\displaystyle\mapsto c+d\ \mathrm{mod}\ m

is a bijection. Then for any infinite almost perfect additive complements E,FE,F, the sets

A=C+m​E,B=D+m​FA=C+mE,\ B=D+mF

are also almost perfect. For example, consider m=4,C={0,2},D={0,3}m=4,C=\{0,2\},D=\{0,3\}, then 1∉A+B1\not\in A+B and A,BA,B are not perfect. We can start the operation with E,FE,F any infinite perfect additive complements, and the examples satisfy r⁡(n)⩽1r(n)\leqslant 1 for all nn. We have not found the example of almost perfect additive complements with r⁡(n)⩾2r(n)\geqslant 2 for some nn.

Note that almost perfect implies eventually unique, but the reverse remains open. As in Lemma 2.1,

A⁡(x)​B​(x)−x↛∞⟹r⁡(n)=1​for sufficiently large​n.A(x)B(x)-x\not\to\infty\implies r(n)=1\ \text{for sufficiently large}\ n.

We are not sure whether the two conditions are equivalent. It is true for the case of infinite perfect additive complements; If one of A,BA,B is finite, the equivalence is trivial. However, we have not found a proof for infinite sets.

Question 5.1.

For infinite additive complements A,BA,B with r⁡(n)=1r(n)=1 for all large nn, is it true that lim infn(A⁡(n)​B​(n)−n)<∞\liminf_{n}(A(n)B(n)-n)<\infty?

5.2. The main theorem

(3.3) is a bridge from the combinatorial problem to the analysis problem. It relies on the relation

(5.1) r⁡(n)=1,n>n0;r(n)=1,n>n_{0};
(5.2) 𝒞⁡(Nj)=O⁡(1),for some subsequence​{Nj}.\mathcal{C}(N_{j})=O(1),\ \text{for some subsequence}\ \{N_{j}\}.

Recall that for additive complements A,BA,B,

A⁡(N)​B​(N)−N=∑0⩽n⩽N(r⁡(n)−1)+𝒞⁡(N)+1.A(N)B(N)-N=\sum_{0\leqslant n\leqslant N}(r(n)-1)+\mathcal{C}(N)+1.

Hence A⁡(x)​B​(x)−x↛∞A(x)B(x)-x\not\to\infty is equivalent to (5.1)(5.2) taken together. It is easy to find a counterexample to show that (5.2) does not imply (5.1). It remains open whether (5.1) alone implies (5.2), as shown in Question 5.1.

A strong result is obtainable with the full power of Gabardo–Lai theorem and a similar argument in Section 3. We skip the details.

Theorem 5.2.

Fix the complementary pair (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) given in (3.4)(3.5) and let {Mk}\{M_{k}\} be the integer sequence associated with the complementary pair [9, Thm. 2.2].

(i)(i) In the Type I (finite) case,

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x=2.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}=2.

(i​i)(ii) In the Type II (infinite) case,

lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x⩾2​Mk+2Mk+2,k⩾2.\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\geqslant\frac{2M_{k}+2}{M_{k}+2},k\geqslant 2.

Particularly, the upper limit is ⩾8/5\geqslant 8/5 if Mk⩾3M_{k}\geqslant 3 for some k⩾2k\geqslant 2, and equals 22 for unbounded {Mk}\{M_{k}\}.

In fact, we can get a better lower bound with more information on {Mk}\{M_{k}\}. However, since we simply choose a specific subsequence {Nj}\{N_{j}\} and lose some information, the idea is only available to obtain the lower bound of the upper limit instead of the exact value. Furthermore, we are not able to rule out the following case: Consider the sequence {dk}\{d_{k}\} defined by

dk={3,k=n2​for some integer​n,2,otherwise.d_{k}=\begin{cases}3,\ k=n^{2}\ \text{for some integer}\ n,\\ 2,\ \text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

It is possible to choose a bad subsequence, for example Nj=∏k⩽j⁡(j+1)−1dk−1N_{j}=\prod_{k\leqslant j(j+1)-1}d_{k}-1, such that the corresponding Gabardo–Lai sequence {Mk}\{M_{k}\} satisfies Mk=2M_{k}=2 for all kk. Then we are only able to get a lower bound of 3/23/2 but no gaps on the right side of 3/23/2, while the exact value for this example is 18/11>8/518/11>8/5.

Another problem for us is to find a purely combinatorial method for the result. Thanks to Zhang [15], we know that the discrete proof does exist.

5.3. Miscellaneous

In Gabardo and Lai’s paper [9], they gave a new proof of the classification of perfect additive complements for finite sets {0,1,…,N−1}\{0,1,\ldots,N-1\} with their convolution decomposition theorem.

The second moment in the proof of Lemma 2.2 is sometimes called the additive energy, which is useful in some combinatorial problems.

Bárány, Fang and Sándor treated the problem from a different point of view. Our Theorem 4.5 gives an elementary proof of the consequence of [1, Lemma 4.3], and a similar result follows.

Theorem 5.3.

Let A,BA,B be additive complements associated with {dk},dk∈ℤ⩾2\{d_{k}\},d_{k}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geqslant 2}. If

lim supkdk=G,lim infkdk=g,\limsup_{k}d_{k}=G,\ \liminf_{k}d_{k}=g,

with 2⩽g⩽G<∞2\leqslant g\leqslant G<\infty, then

lim infk→∞Dk∈[g−1g​G−1,1G+1].\liminf_{k\to\infty}D_{k}\in\Big[\frac{g-1}{gG-1},\frac{1}{G+1}\Big].

Fix an integer G⩾3G\geqslant 3. Consider the spectrum with parameter GG:

𝔏G:={lim supx→∞A⁡(x)​B​(x)x∣A,Bassociated with{dk},lim supkdk=G}⊆[2−2G+2,2−1G].\mathfrak{L}_{G}:=\Big\{\limsup_{x\to\infty}\frac{A(x)B(x)}{x}\mid A,B\ \text{associated with}\ \{d_{k}\},\limsup_{k}d_{k}=G\Big\}\subseteq\Big[2-\frac{2}{G+2},2-\frac{1}{G}\Big].

This will lead to the further problem concerning the structure. The following is an example and was partially solved by Bárány, Fang and Sándor [1].

Question 5.4.

Decide all accumulation points of the spectrum 𝔏G\mathfrak{L}_{G}.
